lesson_title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports
claim_text: Padel is a racket sport… It originated in Mexico in the 1960s.
issue: Accurate in substance — padel was invented in 1969 in Acapulco, Mexico by Enrique Corcuera. The '1960s' phrasing is technically imprecise (1969 is widely cited as the founding year) but not wrong as a decade. The lesson does not give the specific year 1969 or name Acapulco, which are the details the specification and common textbooks cite. No error but imprecision.
correct_version: Padel originated in 1969 in Acapulco, Mexico, invented by Enrique Corcuera. The LTA — not a body called 'Padel England' — became the national governing body for padel in Britain.

lesson_title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports
claim_text: Padel England secured recognition as the national governing body and affiliated to the Lawn Tennis Association for development support.
issue: Incorrect entity name and incorrect relationship. The LTA (Lawn Tennis Association) is itself the national governing body for padel in Britain — it was announced as such by Sport England, Sport Scotland and Sport Wales. There is no separate body called 'Padel England' that affiliated to the LTA; rather, LTA Padel (formerly British Padel) operates under the LTA umbrella. The description implies two separate organisations with a subordinate relationship, which is wrong.
correct_version: The LTA (Lawn Tennis Association) was confirmed as the national governing body for padel in Britain by Sport England, Sport Scotland and Sport Wales. LTA Padel (formerly British Padel) is the padel arm within the LTA structure.

lesson_title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports
claim_text: In 2024, Sport England formally recognised Pickleball England as the sport's national governing body.
issue: Plausible claim but the exact recognition year and the exact name 'Pickleball England' could not be independently confirmed via Sport England's published records in this search. USA Pickleball and Pickleball England are separate bodies. The claim is within the zone of plausibility but carries hallucination risk. No clear error found, flagged as low-severity for editorial awareness.
correct_version: If confirmed, the year and body name should be cited from Sport England's official recognition list.
source: Unable to verify exact date/name from Sport England official list. Pickleball history: https://usapickleball.org/news/how-pickleball-got-its-name/

lesson_title: Popularity of Sport in the UK & Emerging Sports
claim_text: Emma Raducanu's 2021 US Open victory produced a 46% increase in tennis court bookings in the following months.
issue: The '46%' figure is specific and unverified. News sources confirm a documented surge in tennis participation and court demand following Raducanu's win (the 'Raducanu effect' was widely reported, and LTA data showed participation rises). However, the precise 46% figure for court bookings specifically could not be confirmed from LTA, Sport England, or news sources. It may be a fabricated statistic or a misremembered figure.
correct_version: A documented surge in court bookings and grassroots tennis sign-ups followed Raducanu's 2021 US Open win. The LTA reported participation increases; one source cited ~100,000 new players in the two months following the win. The exact '46%' figure for court bookings is unverified and should be removed or sourced.

lesson_title: Values in Sport — Team Spirit, Fair Play & National Pride
claim_text: The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius — Communiter' (Faster, Higher, Stronger — Together) captures this value.
issue: The motto wording and Latin translation are correct. The word 'Communiter' (Together) was indeed added in July 2021 during the IOC Session before the Tokyo Games, approved unanimously. The lesson accurately reflects the current full motto. No error.
correct_version: Correct. 'Communiter' added 20 July 2021 by unanimous IOC Session vote.

lesson_title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
claim_text: This creed is attributed to Bishop Ethelbert Talbot (1908) and was later adopted by Pierre de Coubertin as the guiding philosophy of the Games.
issue: Attribution is broadly correct. Bishop Ethelbert Talbot of Central Pennsylvania (not Pennsylvania generally) delivered a sermon at St Paul's Cathedral during the 1908 London Games which inspired Coubertin's formulation of the creed. The name 'Ethelbert Talbot' and the year 1908 are accurate. The IOC sources confirm this attribution. No material error.
correct_version: Correct attribution. The Bishop's full title was Bishop of Central Pennsylvania. The IOC confirms Talbot's 1908 sermon as the inspiration.

lesson_title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
claim_text: The Olympic symbol consists of five interlocking rings… Designed by Pierre de Coubertin and first used in 1913.
issue: The design date of 1913 is confirmed — Coubertin created the rings in 1913 and they first appeared on his letterhead that year. However, the rings were NOT first used publicly at a Games in 1913 — they made their Olympic Games debut at Antwerp 1920. The lesson's phrasing 'first used in 1913' is ambiguous: 1913 is correct for the design/letterhead first appearance, but 1920 for first use at the Olympic Games. For GCSE purposes this is likely acceptable but could mislead students into thinking the rings appeared at a pre-1920 Games.
correct_version: Rings designed in 1913 (first on Coubertin's letterhead), first publicly presented as an Olympic symbol in 1914 (Olympic Congress, Paris), first used at the Games in Antwerp 1920.

lesson_title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
claim_text: Paris last hosted the summer Olympics in 1900; it returned in 2024 after 100 years.
issue: FACTUALLY WRONG. Paris previously hosted the Summer Olympics in both 1900 AND 1924. The most recent previous hosting before 2024 was Paris 1924, a gap of 100 years — not the 1900 Games. The lesson explicitly states '1900' as the last previous hosting, which is incorrect. The correct prior Games were Paris 1924, meaning 2024 was Paris's third hosting of the Summer Olympics.
correct_version: Paris last hosted the Summer Olympics in 1924 (not 1900), returning in 2024 after exactly 100 years. It was Paris's third time hosting the Summer Games (1900, 1924, 2024).

lesson_title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
claim_text: Olympic values (three): Excellence, Respect, Friendship. Paralympic values (four): Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality.
issue: Both value sets are correct as stated. The IOC lists three Olympic values (Excellence, Respect, Friendship) and the IPC lists four Paralympic values (Courage, Determination, Inspiration, Equality). No error.
correct_version: Correct.

lesson_title: The Olympic & Paralympic Movement
claim_text: The Olympic Village at Paris 2024 housed over 14,500 athletes from 206 nations.
issue: The figure of 206 nations is consistent with IOC membership and standard Games participation counts. 14,500 athletes is a plausible figure for the combined Olympic and Paralympic athletes; the Olympic Games alone had around 10,714 athletes. The combined 14,500 estimate is cited in some sources when including athletes from both Games. No clear error but the figure merits editorial awareness.
correct_version: The 2024 Paris Olympic Games had approximately 10,714 athletes from 206 delegations. Combined with Paralympic athletes the Village figure of ~14,500 is plausible.

lesson_title: Etiquette, Sportsmanship & Spectator Behaviour
claim_text: Following the Hillsborough disaster in 1989 — where 97 Liverpool supporters lost their lives in a crowd crush.
issue: The death toll figure requires careful handling. At the time of the Taylor Report (1990), 95 people had died. The 96th victim (Tony Bland) died in 1993. The 97th victim (Andrew Devine) died in 2021. The lesson's use of '97' is technically the ultimate total, but the Taylor Report itself was written when only 95 had died, and the widely cited pre-2021 figure was 96. A GCSE lesson written before 2021 would say 96; after 2021 it is accurate to say 97. Using '97' without context is potentially misleading for students who encounter 'the 96' in other sources (e.g., Liverpool FC tributes, the Justice for the 96 campaign name). The lesson should note both figures and the timeline.
correct_version: The disaster in April 1989 initially killed 95 people; a 96th victim died in 1993 and a 97th in 2021. The campaign was historically known as 'Justice for the 96'. As of 2021 the official death toll is 97. The lesson's use of '97' is factually accurate for the final total but should be contextualised. Not a hard error but potentially confusing without context.

lesson_title: Etiquette, Sportsmanship & Spectator Behaviour
claim_text: Lord Justice Taylor produced the Taylor Report (1990). Its central recommendation was that top-flight football grounds in England should become all-seater stadia. By 1994–95, all Premier League and First Division grounds had converted.
issue: The Taylor Report date (1990), the all-seater recommendation, and the 1994-95 compliance deadline are all accurate. The final Taylor Report was published in January 1990. The Football League required all-seater conversion by August 1994 (in time for 1994-95 season). No error.
correct_version: Correct.

lesson_title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
claim_text: The nine categories on the Prohibited List include: anabolic agents, peptide hormones, beta blockers, stimulants, diuretics, narcotics, cannabinoids, glucocorticoids, and alcohol (in certain sports).
issue: Multiple errors in the category list. The WADA Prohibited List has 10 substance categories (S0–S9) plus 3 prohibited method categories (M1–M3) plus one sport-specific category (P1). The lesson's list of 'nine categories' is wrong in both count and composition. Key errors: (1) Beta-2 Agonists (S3) are omitted — replaced incorrectly by 'beta blockers'; (2) Beta-blockers are NOT a general banned substance — they are a sport-specific category (P1) prohibited only in certain sports such as archery and shooting; (3) 'Hormone and Metabolic Modulators' (S4) is omitted; (4) 'Non-Approved Substances' (S0) is omitted; (5) Alcohol (P2 in some older versions) is not a current headline substance category in the way presented. The list mixes up beta blockers (sport-specific) with beta-2 agonists (general) — a significant error that could cost exam marks.
correct_version: The WADA Prohibited List substance categories are S0 Non-Approved Substances, S1 Anabolic Agents, S2 Peptide Hormones/Growth Factors, S3 Beta-2 Agonists, S4 Hormone and Metabolic Modulators, S5 Diuretics and Masking Agents, S6 Stimulants, S7 Narcotics, S8 Cannabinoids, S9 Glucocorticoids. Beta-blockers (P1) are prohibited only in specific sports (archery, shooting, golf etc.), not universally. The lesson incorrectly lists 'beta blockers' as a general category and omits 'beta-2 agonists', 'hormone and metabolic modulators', and 'non-approved substances'.

lesson_title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
claim_text: WADA was founded in 1999.
issue: Correct. WADA was established on 10 November 1999 in Lausanne following the World Conference on Doping in Sport held in February 1999.
correct_version: Correct.

lesson_title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
claim_text: If an athlete accumulates three missed tests or filing failures within any 12-month rolling period, this counts as an anti-doping rule violation.
issue: Correct. The WADA Whereabouts Rules state that three whereabouts failures (missed tests and/or filing failures) in any rolling 12-month period constitutes an anti-doping rule violation (Article 2.4 of the WADA Code). No error.
correct_version: Correct.

lesson_title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
claim_text: Swimmer Sun Yang received an eight-year ban (later revised on appeal) for refusing to cooperate with anti-doping testers.
issue: Broadly accurate but imprecise. Sun Yang was given an eight-year ban in February 2020 by CAS for tampering with doping control (his security guard smashed sample containers). The Swiss Federal Tribunal overturned this in December 2020 on procedural grounds (panel chair bias). A second CAS panel in June 2021 reduced the ban to four years and three months. The lesson's description 'later revised on appeal' is accurate but omits the complexity: the ban was overturned then re-imposed at a reduced level. The characterisation 'refusing to cooperate' is an oversimplification — the violation was 'tampering with doping control' (smashing the vials), not simply refusing.
correct_version: Sun Yang received an eight-year ban in February 2020 for tampering with doping control (sample containers were smashed). This was overturned on procedural grounds by the Swiss Federal Tribunal in December 2020, then a new CAS panel in June 2021 imposed a revised ban of four years and three months. The violation was tampering, not merely 'refusing to cooperate'.

lesson_title: Performance-Enhancing Drugs, WADA & Sanctions
claim_text: Russia's track and field athletes were barred from competing under the Russian flag at the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympics as a direct result of a state-sponsored doping programme.
issue: Partially inaccurate. Russian athletes in most sports at Paris 2024 could compete as AIN (Individual Neutral Athletes — Athlètes Individuels Neutres), not simply 'barred'. However, Russian and Belarusian track and field athletes were specifically barred from Paris 2024 by World Athletics (which maintained its suspension separately from the IOC's AIN pathway). The lesson conflates two different situations: (a) general Russian Olympic participation was as AIN neutrals; (b) specifically in athletics, Russian athletes were barred outright by World Athletics. The claim that they were 'barred' is accurate for athletics specifically, but the lesson's phrasing implies a blanket ban across all sports which is not the case for Paris 2024.
correct_version: At Paris 2024, Russian athletes in most sports could compete as Individual Neutral Athletes (AIN) under strict eligibility conditions. However, Russian track and field athletes were barred outright by World Athletics which maintained a separate suspension. At Tokyo 2020, Russian athletes competed as ROC (Russian Olympic Committee) following WADA sanctions.

lesson_title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding
claim_text: The 2024 Paris Games sold over 9 million tickets.
issue: Correct in substance. Paris 2024 sold a record 9.7 million tickets (8.7 million for the Olympics, 1 million for the Paralympics), surpassing the previous record of 8.3 million from Atlanta 1996. 'Over 9 million' is accurate.
correct_version: Correct. 9.7 million tickets were sold across both the Olympic and Paralympic Games.

lesson_title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding
claim_text: The Paris 2024 Games budget grew from an initial estimate of around 3.6 billion euros to approximately 8.8 billion euros by the time the Games opened.
issue: The figures are not accurate. The organizing committee (COJO) budget reached €4.48 billion. Total French state expenditure (including infrastructure and security) was €6.6 billion by auditor estimates published in 2025. The figure of '8.8 billion euros' does not match any authoritative published total. The initial estimate of '3.6 billion euros' does not correspond to any widely reported official figure — the initial public contribution cap was stated as around €1 billion; the infrastructure budget was around €3.6 billion. Using '3.6 billion' to represent the total initial budget misrepresents the cost structure.
correct_version: The Paris 2024 organizing committee (COJO) budget was approximately €4.48 billion. Total French state spending including infrastructure was around €6.6 billion (French Court of Auditors, 2025). An '8.8 billion' total is not supported by authoritative sources. The lesson's figures should be revised or cited to a specific source.

lesson_title: Hosting a Major Sporting Event — Pre-Event & Bidding
claim_text: The opening ceremony along the Seine attracting a global television audience estimated at 1.5 billion viewers.
issue: The 1.5 billion figure cannot be confirmed. Verified regional figures show 24.4 million viewers in France and 28.6 million on NBCUniversal platforms in the USA. The IOC claimed record overall Games audiences but did not publish a 1.5 billion opening-ceremony-specific figure in available sources. This appears to be an inflated or fabricated statistic. The IOC's overall Paris 2024 total cumulative audience was reported as reaching around 3 billion across all platforms and all days of the Games — but that is very different from 1.5 billion for the opening ceremony alone.
correct_version: No authoritative source confirms 1.5 billion television viewers for the opening ceremony. Regional peak figures were: ~24 million (France), ~28 million (USA). The overall Games audience was broadly described as record-breaking by the IOC. The '1.5 billion' figure should be removed or replaced with a verifiable claim.

lesson_title: Hosting a Major Event — During & After (Legacy)
claim_text: The Athens 2004 Olympics is the most cited cautionary example… The estimated cost of the Athens Games was around £7–9 billion.
issue: The figure is in the right zone but slightly imprecise in currency. The Athens 2004 Games cost approximately €9 billion / ~$11–12 billion. Expressing this as '£7–9 billion' is a rough currency conversion that approximates the figure; at 2004 exchange rates €9bn was roughly £6–7 billion, so '£7–9 billion' may be slightly overstated. The lesson's figure is not wildly wrong but the currency conversion is imprecise.
correct_version: Athens 2004 cost approximately €9 billion (or ~$11–12 billion at the time). In sterling at 2004 exchange rates this was approximately £6–7 billion. The lesson's '£7–9 billion' is at the high end of reasonable estimates.

lesson_title: Hosting a Major Event — During & After (Legacy)
claim_text: The Paris 2024 Games deployed 45,000 security personnel and involved NATO partner support.
issue: The 45,000 figure for security personnel is consistent with widely reported pre-Games planning figures (France announced 45,000 police and gendarmerie plus additional private security and military). NATO partner support involvement at the Games has been reported in security contexts. The claim is broadly accurate.
correct_version: Broadly accurate. France deployed approximately 45,000 security forces (police and gendarmerie) plus additional private security and military personnel.
source: Multiple news sources confirmed 45,000+ security personnel for Paris 2024.

lesson_title: National Governing Bodies & Technology in Sport
claim_text: LTA (Lawn Tennis Association, governing tennis in Great Britain). ECB (England and Wales Cricket Board, governing cricket). RFU (Rugby Football Union, governing rugby union in England). The FA (Football Association, governing football in England).
issue: All four NGB descriptions are correct. LTA governs tennis in Great Britain, Channel Islands and Isle of Man. ECB governs cricket in England and Wales. RFU governs rugby union in England. The FA governs football in England. No errors.
correct_version: Correct as stated.

lesson_title: National Governing Bodies & Technology in Sport
claim_text: VAR (Video Assistant Referee) was introduced into the Premier League in the 2019–20 season.
issue: Correct. VAR was introduced into the Premier League for the 2019-20 season, approved by clubs in November 2018 and first used in the opening match of the season (Liverpool vs Norwich, August 2019). No error.
correct_version: Correct.
